tagline: A great poem about an innocent man who loses everything, argues with his friends and with God, and meets God in the storm.
overview:
Job is the Bible's longest and most searching treatment of innocent suffering. A short prose story frames it: Job, a wealthy and godly man from the land of Uz, loses his flocks, his servants, his ten children, and finally his health, because God has allowed the accuser to test whether Job's devotion is real or merely paid for. The reader is told this from the start. Job never is.

Between the prose opening and the prose ending lies a long poem. Job curses the day he was born. Three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar, come to comfort him and end up arguing that suffering like his must be punishment for sin, so he should repent. Job refuses to confess what he hasn't done, and he turns from them to God, demanding a hearing. A younger man, Elihu, adds four speeches of his own. Then the LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind, not with an explanation of the test but with a tour of creation, from the foundations of the earth to the wild animals and the great beasts Behemoth and Leviathan. Job falls silent, retracts his words, and the story closes with God rebuking the friends, saying that Job has spoken rightly of him, and restoring Job's fortunes.

The book matters because it refuses the easy answers. It denies that all suffering is deserved, it lets a righteous man protest to God at length and in the Bible's own pages, and it ends not with a theory of evil but with an encounter. Generations of readers, believers and unbelievers alike, have found in it the most honest words ever written about pain.
author: The book doesn't name its author, and no other part of the Bible says who wrote it. A Jewish tradition recorded in the Babylonian Talmud credits Moses, which fits the book's patriarchal feel: Job offers sacrifices himself as head of his family, measures wealth in flocks and herds, and lives 140 years after his restoration. The same Talmudic discussion (Bava Batra 15a) records other opinions too, placing Job in various eras, and includes one rabbi's view that Job never existed and that the book is a mashal, a parable told to teach. Most modern scholars, conservative and critical alike, think the author was an unnamed Israelite poet of great learning, writing in a Hebrew rich with rare words and with many Aramaic features, and drawing on a story about Job that may have been older than the poem. Some critical scholars also think the book grew in stages, with the Elihu speeches (chapters 32 to 37) and the poem on wisdom (chapter 28) added later, while others argue that the book as it stands shows a single design. What is clear is that the writer knew the wisdom traditions of Israel and its neighbors and wrote the most demanding poetry in the Old Testament.
date: There are two questions: when Job lived and when the book was written. The story is set in a world like that of the patriarchs, with no mention of Israel, the exodus, the law of Moses, the temple, or the kings, and Ezekiel mentions Job alongside Noah and Daniel as a famous righteous man of old (Ezekiel 14:14, 20). The writing of the book is harder to fix. Proposals range from the time of Solomon (tenth century BC), when Israel's wisdom writing flourished, through the seventh century, to the period after the Babylonian exile (sixth to fourth centuries BC), a view often argued from the book's language and its reflection on undeserved suffering. Copies and fragments of Job, including an Aramaic translation, were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, so the book was complete and in use well before the time of Jesus. The honest answer is that the date of writing is unknown and the positions are held by capable scholars on each side.
setting:
Job lives in Uz, a land east of Israel whose exact location is uncertain. Lamentations 4:21 links Uz with Edom, south and east of the Dead Sea, and some scholars look instead to the regions north and east toward Aram. The friends come from places with Edomite and Arabian associations: Eliphaz is a Temanite, and Teman was an Edomite clan descended from Esau (Genesis 36:11); Bildad is a Shuhite, and Shuah was a son of Abraham by Keturah (Genesis 25:2). Job himself is not an Israelite. The raiders who strike his household, the Sabeans and Chaldeans, are desert and border peoples, and the caravans of Tema and Sheba (6:19) belong to the Arabian trade routes.

The wider world of the book is the ancient Near East, where wise men in several cultures wrestled with suffering. Babylonian texts such as the poem often called Ludlul bel nemeqi, in which a devout man describes his affliction and eventual restoration by the god Marduk, and the so-called Babylonian Theodicy, a dialogue between a sufferer and a friend, show that Job's question was not Israel's alone. Job differs from them in its length, its daring, and above all in the God who finally speaks.
purpose: Job was written to test and deepen the wisdom tradition, not to overturn it. Books like Proverbs teach that the righteous generally flourish and the wicked generally fall, which is true as a pattern of God's world. Job asks what happens when the pattern breaks, and it shows what goes wrong when the pattern is turned into a rule that can be run backward: if you are suffering, you must have sinned. The book also asks the question the accuser raises in chapter 1, whether anyone serves God for nothing, and answers it through Job's clinging, protesting faith. For its first readers, and for every reader since, it gives permission to bring grief and complaint straight to God, and it warns comforters against speaking for God more confidently than they know.
story: Job belongs to the Bible's wisdom books, alongside Proverbs and Ecclesiastes, with the Psalms and the Song of Songs close by. It stands somewhat apart from the main storyline that runs from Abraham through Israel's history, since Job is not an Israelite and the covenant with Israel is never mentioned. That is part of its point: the questions it asks belong to every human being under the one creator. Within the whole story, Job stands between the good creation of Genesis, which the LORD's speeches revisit, and the long record of Israel's own suffering in exile, where the question of whether God is just to his people became urgent. The New Testament cites Job's perseverance and the Lord's compassion toward him (James 5:11).
christ: The book does not predict Jesus, and its greatest lines should not be forced into prophecy. But it opens questions that the rest of the Bible answers in Christ. Job longs for a mediator who could stand between him and God (9:33), a witness in heaven (16:19), and a redeemer who lives (19:25); Christians hear in these longings the shape of what God gives in Jesus, the one mediator who is both God and man. Job is an innocent sufferer whom his friends count as a sinner; Jesus is the fully innocent one who was numbered with the transgressors and cried out to God in the words of Psalm 22. The accuser who questions Job's heart before God (in Hebrew ha-satan, a title with the definite article, meaning the accuser or adversary) is read by most Christian interpreters as the same enemy the New Testament says Christ has defeated, though many Old Testament scholars think the figure in Job is a member of the heavenly court whose identification with the devil came later. And where Job's restoration comes at the end of his story, the resurrection of Jesus is the pledge that God's final word over the suffering of the righteous is life.
reading: Read Job as poetry and as drama, not as a set of proof texts. Much of what is said in the book is said by characters the LORD later corrects (42:7), so a verse from Eliphaz, Bildad, or Zophar isn't automatically the book's teaching, even when it sounds pious; watch who is speaking. Read the prologue carefully, because the reader knows what Job doesn't, and that gap drives the whole book. Expect repetition across the three cycles of speeches, and watch how the friends harden and how Job's thought moves. The Hebrew is often obscure, and translations differ more here than almost anywhere else in the Old Testament. The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation, gives a text of Job about a sixth shorter than the Hebrew, a sign of how hard its first translators found the poetry. Common misreadings include treating the heavenly scene as a full explanation of all suffering, treating the friends as simply wicked (they say many true things and apply them wrongly), and treating the happy ending as a reward that makes the losses not matter.

structure.title: Prologue: the test in heaven and on earth
structure.summary: A prose story introduces Job, the scenes in the heavenly court, the loss of his wealth, children, and health, and the arrival of his three friends.

structure.title: Job's lament
structure.summary: Job breaks a seven-day silence by cursing the day of his birth and asking why the miserable are given life.

structure.title: The first cycle of speeches
structure.summary: Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar each speak, and Job answers each one; the friends urge repentance and Job protests his innocence and appeals to God.

structure.title: The second cycle
structure.summary: The friends dwell on the fate of the wicked, and Job, deserted by everyone, reaches toward a witness and a redeemer.

structure.title: The third cycle
structure.summary: Eliphaz accuses Job of specific sins, Bildad gives a short speech, Zophar does not speak, and the debate breaks down.

structure.title: A poem on wisdom
structure.summary: People can mine the earth for treasure but cannot find wisdom; God alone knows its place, and the fear of the Lord is wisdom.

structure.title: Job's final defense
structure.summary: Job remembers his former honor, laments his present shame, and swears a series of oaths of innocence, calling on God to answer.

structure.title: The speeches of Elihu
structure.summary: A younger man, angry at Job and at the friends, argues that God speaks through suffering to warn and to save.

structure.title: The LORD speaks from the whirlwind
structure.summary: God questions Job about creation and its wild creatures, and Job responds in humility and repentance.

structure.title: Epilogue
structure.summary: The LORD rebukes the friends, accepts Job's prayer for them, and restores Job's household and fortunes.

themes.title: Innocent suffering
themes.body: The book's starting point is a man whom God himself calls blameless and upright, and who suffers not because of his sin but because of his righteousness. That fact, given to the reader in chapters 1 and 2, overturns any simple equation of suffering with guilt. The book does not say that no suffering is deserved; it says that not all of it is, and that people who assume otherwise will speak falsely about God.

themes.title: Disinterested faith
themes.body: The accuser's question, whether Job fears God for nothing, is the book's hidden hinge. If faith is only a transaction, it will collapse when the payments stop. Job's losses test whether a human being can love God for God's own sake. His faith is not calm; it protests, accuses, and demands. But it never lets go of God, and the book presents that stubborn holding on as what faith looks like under the weight of loss.

themes.title: The failure of the comforters
themes.body: Eliphaz, Bildad, and Zophar arrive in love and sit with Job in silence for seven days, which is the best thing they do. Once they begin speaking they defend a theology in which God always rewards the good and punishes the wicked in this life, and they apply it to a man they don't understand. In the end God says they have not spoken rightly about him. The book warns every counselor, pastor, and friend against true general principles misapplied to a particular person.

themes.title: Lament and honest speech to God
themes.body: Job curses his birthday, accuses God of treating him as an enemy, and demands a trial. Yet God says at the end that Job, unlike his friends, has spoken what is right. The book shows that complaint addressed to God can be an act of faith, belonging with the lament psalms, and that God would rather hear anguish spoken to him than tidy doctrine spoken about him.

themes.title: God's wisdom in creation
themes.body: The LORD's speeches do not explain the heavenly test. Instead they show Job a world far larger and wilder than any human account of it, full of creatures that serve no human purpose and are still under God's care. The effect is to set Job's suffering inside the wisdom and freedom of the creator, and to move Job from hearing about God to seeing him (42:5).

keyChapters.why: The heavenly scene and the first test introduce the accuser's question and Job's great confession of worship in loss.
Job's lament sets the tone for the poem, bringing raw grief into the open before any argument begins.
Abandoned by friends and family, Job declares that his Redeemer lives and that he will see God.
A poem on the search for wisdom, which only God possesses, and which begins in the fear of the Lord.
Job's final oaths of innocence give a portrait of Old Testament righteousness in private and public life.
The LORD answers from the whirlwind, questioning Job about the foundations of the world.
Job's response, the rebuke of the friends, and the restoration of Job's household bring the book to its close.

parts.body:
Job is the eighteenth book of the Bible. It has forty-two chapters, and it is the Bible's longest and most searching look at innocent suffering.

A short story in prose opens and closes it. Job, a wealthy and godly man from the land of Uz, loses his flocks, his servants, his ten children and then his health. The reader is told why, at least in part: in the heavenly court the accuser has asked whether Job serves God only for what he gets, and God has allowed him to be tested. Job is never told.

Between the opening and the ending stands a long poem. Job curses the day he was born. Three friends, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar, come to comfort him and end by arguing that suffering like his must be punishment for sin, so he should repent. Job will not confess what he has not done, and he turns from them to God, demanding a hearing. A younger man, Elihu, adds four speeches of his own. Then the LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind. He does not explain the test. He shows Job the world, from the foundations of the earth to the wild animals and the great beasts Behemoth and Leviathan. Job falls silent and takes back his words, and the story ends with God rebuking the friends, saying that Job has spoken rightly of him, and restoring Job's household.

The book refuses easy answers. It denies that all suffering is deserved, it lets a righteous man protest to God at length in the Bible's own pages, and it ends not with a theory of evil but with a meeting. Job's own words near the end say what changed: “My ears had heard of You, but now my eyes have seen You” (42:5).

parts.h: Where it sits in the story
parts.body:
Job belongs to the Bible's wisdom books, with Proverbs and Ecclesiastes, and with the Psalms and the Song of Songs close by. In Christian Bibles it comes right after Esther.

It stands somewhat apart from the main storyline that runs from Abraham through Israel's history. Job is not an Israelite, and the book never mentions Abraham, Moses, the covenant, the law, the temple or the kings. That is part of its point. The questions it asks belong to every human being under the one Creator.

Within the whole story, Job stands between the good creation of Genesis, which the LORD's speeches walk through again, and the long record of Israel's own suffering in exile, when the question of whether God is just to his people became urgent. Other books remember Job. Ezekiel names him with Noah and Daniel as a famous righteous man of old (Ezekiel 14:14, 20), and the New Testament holds up his perseverance (James 5:11).

The book does not name its author, and no other part of the Bible says who wrote it. A Jewish tradition recorded in the Babylonian Talmud credits Moses, which fits the book's old-world feel. The same Talmudic discussion (Bava Batra 15a) records other opinions too, placing Job in various eras. Most modern scholars, conservative and critical alike, think the writer was an unnamed Israelite poet of great learning, writing in a Hebrew rich in rare words and with many Aramaic features, and drawing on a story about Job that may have been older than the poem.

Some critical scholars think the book grew in stages, with the speeches of Elihu (chapters 32 to 37) and the poem on wisdom (chapter 28) added later. Others argue that the book as it stands shows a single design.

There are two questions of date: when Job lived and when the book was written. The story is set in a world like that of the patriarchs. Job's wealth is counted in flocks and herds, he offers sacrifices himself as head of his family, and he lives a hundred and forty years after his restoration. The writing is harder to fix. Proposals run from the time of Solomon in the tenth century BC, when Israel's wisdom writing flourished, through the seventh century, to the years after the Babylonian exile, in the sixth to fourth centuries BC, a view often argued from the book's language. Copies and fragments of Job, among them an Aramaic translation, were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls, so the book was complete and in use well before the time of Jesus.

The honest answer is that the date of writing is unknown, and capable scholars hold each position. These notes take no side.

parts.h: Is Job history, a poem, or a drama?
parts.body:
Readers have answered this in three main ways.

Some read Job as the record of a real man and real events. They point out that the book opens like a history, ‘There was a man in the land of Uz whose name was Job’ (1:1), and that Ezekiel names Job beside Noah and Daniel (Ezekiel 14:14, 20) and James names his perseverance (James 5:11) as they would a man who lived.

Others read it as a great poem built on a real man. On this view an old story about Job stood behind the book, and the poet gave the speeches their present form. No one in grief speaks in long, ordered poems of such skill, and the speeches are plainly the work of a poet, whatever happened in Uz.

Others read the whole book as a wisdom drama, written to teach, like a parable. The same Talmudic discussion that credits Moses records one rabbi's view that Job never existed and that the book is a mashal, a parable told to teach. Some who read it this way also see the scenes in heaven as a dramatic device that sets up the book's question rather than a report of what was said there.

Christians who receive Job as God's word hold each of these views. These notes take no side. On any of them the book asks the same question and gives the same answer, and on any of them the friends are wrong and Job's grief is real.

Job is built like a frame around a picture. The prose story of chapters 1 and 2 and of 42:7-17 holds the long poem of 3:1 to 42:6.

The poem moves in stages. Job's lament opens it (chapter 3). Then come three cycles of speeches. In each, Eliphaz, Bildad and Zophar speak in turn, and Job answers each one (chapters 4 to 14, 15 to 21, and 22 to 27). In the third cycle the debate breaks down: Bildad's speech is short and Zophar does not speak at all. A poem on wisdom follows (chapter 28), then Job's final defense, ending in oaths of innocence (chapters 29 to 31). Elihu speaks next (chapters 32 to 37). Then the LORD speaks twice from the whirlwind, and Job answers twice (38:1 to 42:6).

Two things help a reader. First, watch who is speaking. Much of what is said in the book is said by people the LORD later corrects (42:7), so a verse from Eliphaz, Bildad or Zophar is not the book's teaching just because it sounds devout. Second, expect hard Hebrew. The poetry is full of rare words, and translations differ more here than almost anywhere else in the Old Testament. The ancient Greek translation gives a text about a sixth shorter than the Hebrew, a sign of how hard its first translators found it.

parts.h: The test in heaven, and the accuser
parts.body:
The book lets the reader into a scene Job never sees. The heavenly beings come before the LORD, and among them comes one the Hebrew calls ha-satan, the accuser or adversary, a title with the definite article. The LORD points to Job: “Have you considered My servant Job? For there is no one on earth like him, a man who is blameless and upright, who fears God and shuns evil” (1:8). The accuser answers with the question the whole book turns on: “Does Job fear God for nothing?” (1:9).

Is faith only a bargain, kept while the payments come? The accuser is allowed to strike all Job has, and then his body, but not his life. The book says plainly that the accuser can act only with the LORD's permission and within the limit the LORD sets. It does not let God off the hook either: Job says the LORD has taken away, and the narrator says he did not sin in saying so.

Readers differ on who the accuser is. Some scholars hold that he is a member of the heavenly court whose role is to test and accuse, a prosecutor, not yet the fully developed figure of the devil; they note the definite article and that the word is used of human adversaries elsewhere. Most Christian interpreters, following the New Testament's picture of the accuser, identify him with Satan, the enemy of God. Either way, he is under God's authority and acts with hostile intent toward Job. These notes take no side.

Readers also differ on how literally to take the dialogue in heaven, a real glimpse into God's council or a dramatic device. And one more thing needs saying plainly. The scene explains Job's suffering to the reader. It does not claim to explain every human loss, and it gives no one the right to say of any sufferer that God is testing them or that they are failing a test.

parts.h: Ten children, and a man in the ashes
parts.body:
In one day four messengers come, each while the one before is still speaking. Raiders take the oxen and donkeys and kill the servants. Fire falls on the sheep. Raiders take the camels. Then a great wind strikes the house where Job's sons and daughters are feasting, and all ten die. The book tells it in a few lines and does not linger, and these notes will not either.

Job tears his robe, shaves his head and falls to the ground, the old signs of grief. Then he worships: “Naked I came from my mother’s womb, and naked I will return. The LORD gave, and the LORD has taken away. Blessed be the name of the LORD” (1:21). Later he is struck with painful sores from head to foot and sits in the ashes, the place of mourning and of the outcast. His wife, who has lost the same ten children, tells him, “Curse God and die!” (2:9). Readers have often judged her harshly; many now hear a grieving mother's despair rather than malice.

The friends come, weep aloud, tear their robes and sit on the ground with him for seven days and nights, ‘but no one spoke a word to him because they saw how intense his suffering was’ (2:13). It is the best thing they do.

Job's worship in 1:21 is not the whole of his grief. In the next chapter he curses the day he was born. The book holds both, and so may anyone who grieves.

Grief is not a lack of faith. If your grief is so heavy that you cannot carry it, please tell someone: a pastor, a friend, a doctor or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

If you carry grief or guilt about a pregnancy, or about the loss of a child before or after birth, please know that you are met with gentleness here, not judgment. God knows your story too. Please talk with a trusted pastor or friend. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

parts.h: Job's lament: the day of his birth
parts.body:
After seven days Job speaks, and his first words are a curse on the day of his birth: “May the day of my birth perish” (3:3). He asks, “Why did I not perish at birth; why did I not die as I came from the womb?” (3:11). He pictures the grave as rest, where the weary and the prisoner are at peace, and he asks the question many sufferers have asked: “Why is light given to the miserable, and life to the bitter of soul, who long for death that does not come” (3:20-21).

He does not curse God, as the accuser predicted. He curses his own existence. The book does not scold him for it, and it does not cut the words out. Jeremiah says the same kind of thing (Jeremiah 20:14-18), and the Psalms hold laments as dark as this one, Psalm 88 among them. At the end the LORD says that Job has spoken rightly of him (42:7). Readers have long concluded that honest lament spoken in God's hearing is not condemned.

The book does not end here, though. Job's lament is the beginning of a long struggle that brings him at last to meet God. The words are given to put pain into speech, not to be the last word.

If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country. If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

parts.h: The friends' case, and the book's verdict on it
parts.body:
The friends are not villains. They leave their own homes to come to him, they weep, they sit in silence for a week. And much of what they say is true in general. God is just. He opposes the wicked. Human beings are frail, and no one is perfectly righteous before God. Proverbs and the Psalms say the same.

Their case, put in the form they would sign, runs like this. God is just and rules the world. A just God does not punish the innocent. So suffering like Job's must answer to some sin, perhaps one he does not know. The kindest thing a friend can do is say so, and urge him to turn back to God, who forgives and restores. Eliphaz says it gently at first: “Consider now, I plead: Who, being innocent, has ever perished?” (4:7). Bildad and Zophar say it harder. In the third cycle Eliphaz lists sins Job must have committed, crimes against widows, orphans and the poor, though nothing in the book supports the charge.

The book's verdict comes from God: “My wrath is kindled against you and your two friends. For you have not spoken about Me accurately, as My servant Job has” (42:7). Their error was not that every sentence was false. It was that they turned a pattern into a rule and ran it backward, from suffering to sin. They trusted their account of God more than the man in front of them, and they spoke for God with more certainty than they had.

The book does not let anyone speak to a sufferer as they did. No one may tell a grieving person that their loss is a punishment, or that they are suffering because of some sin they must find, or that they are failing a test. Job's friends did that, and God called it folly (42:8).

parts.h: Job's protest: a mediator, a witness, a Redeemer
parts.body:
Job's speeches are not calm. He accuses God of treating him as an enemy, he demands a trial, and he swears that he is innocent. He will not confess sins he has not committed, even to end his suffering. But he never stops speaking to God, and the book presents that stubborn holding on as what faith looks like under the weight of loss.

His hope grows as he speaks. Early on he says there is no umpire between him and God: “Nor is there a mediator between us, to lay his hand upon us both” (9:33). Later he says, “Even now my witness is in heaven, and my advocate is on high” (16:19). Then, deserted by his brothers, his friends, his servants and his wife, he says the book's most famous words: “But I know that my Redeemer lives, and in the end He will stand upon the earth” (19:25). The Redeemer, go'el in Hebrew, was the nearest relative who stood up for a family member in trouble. Job has no human go'el left, and he says he has one who lives.

Readers differ on whom Job means, and on how far he sees. Many think he means God himself, appealing from God as accuser to God as defender. Others think he pictures a heavenly figure distinct from God who will plead for him. The Hebrew of the next lines is hard: the phrase rendered ‘in my flesh’ (19:26) can also be translated apart from the flesh, and the timing is unclear. Some read them as hope of bodily resurrection, some as hope of being cleared after death without resurrection, and some as hope of seeing God before death, which is what happens in chapter 42. Christians have long read the verse in the light of Christ, while recognizing that Job could not have known of Jesus, and the New Testament does not quote it. What is not in doubt is Job's certainty that he will see God for himself.

parts.h: Where wisdom is found, and Job's last defense
parts.body:
Chapter 28 is a poem of a different tone, calm where the speeches are anguished. People can dig into the earth for silver, gold and jewels, going where no bird has flown. But wisdom cannot be mined, bought or found anywhere in the world. God alone knows the way to it, and he has told humanity what it is: ‘the fear of the Lord, that is wisdom, and to turn away from evil is understanding’ (28:28).

Readers differ on who speaks it. In the text as it stands Job does, since no new speaker is named. Many interpreters think it is an interlude from the book's narrator, commenting on the failed debate. Others see it as Job's own moment of calm insight, or as a preview of what God's speeches will show. On any view it stands near the center of the book and names its deepest theme.

Then Job speaks his last defense (chapters 29 to 31). He remembers his honor, when he was ‘a father to the needy’ (29:16). He laments his shame now. And he swears a series of oaths that he has not lied, lusted, cheated his servants, ignored the poor or trusted in gold, and he signs his case and waits for God to answer.

Then a new voice. Elihu, a younger man who has been listening, is angry with Job for justifying himself rather than God, and angry with the friends for condemning Job without answering him. He speaks for six chapters. His new thought is that God may speak through suffering, to warn, to discipline and to save. He ends describing a storm breaking, which leads straight into the LORD's own speech from the whirlwind.

Readers have long disagreed about him. Some see a wise voice who corrects both Job and the friends and prepares the way for God; they note that God does not rebuke him at the end, when he rebukes the three friends (42:7-9). Others see a young man who repeats the friends' arguments at greater length; they point to his long self-introduction, his anger, and the fact that God, when he speaks, ignores Elihu entirely. Still others think his speeches were added to the book later, since he is missing from the prologue and the epilogue and his style differs. Some think the book means him to be both right and wrong in part. The text does not settle it, and these notes take no side.

What is clear is that Elihu's words, like the friends', are a human speaker's, to be weighed. Even where he is right that God can teach through hardship, he does not claim that anyone can tell what God is doing in a particular person's loss, and no reader should.

parts.h: The LORD answers from the whirlwind
parts.body:
‘Then the LORD answered Job out of the whirlwind’ (38:1). God comes, as Job asked, and speaks to him personally. But he asks the questions: “Where were you when I laid the foundations of the earth? Tell Me, if you have understanding” (38:4). He walks Job through creation, the sea held behind its doors, the morning, the storehouses of snow, the stars, and then the wild animals: the lion and the raven fed, the mountain goat giving birth unseen, the wild donkey, the ostrich, the war horse, the hawk. Much of it concerns places no human goes and creatures that serve no human purpose, cared for because God made them.

In a second speech God asks, “Would you condemn Me to justify yourself?” (40:8), and points to two great beasts. Behemoth, whose name means the beast of beasts, lies among the reeds unafraid of the raging river. Leviathan, in the sea, can be caught by no hook and wounded by no weapon. Many scholars identify Behemoth with the hippopotamus and Leviathan with the crocodile, described in heightened language. Others see mythic creatures of chaos, as Leviathan is elsewhere in the Bible, and as a serpent called Litan is in older poems from Ugarit. Many take a middle path: real animals, described in the language of chaos, so that the most fearsome things on earth stand before God as his creatures. Some have proposed that Behemoth was a dinosaur; most scholars read the text otherwise. These notes take no side.

What do the speeches answer? Readers differ here too. Some critics hear raw power silencing a man who asked a fair question. Others hear something different: God comes, he is not hostile, and he corrects the idea Job and his friends shared, that the world runs by a simple rule of reward and punishment that humans can inspect. What the speeches do not do is plain to every reader. They never mention the test in heaven, and they never tell Job why he suffered. The book shows that Job did not know the reasons, that God did, and that meeting God proved enough for Job without them.

parts.h: Dust and ashes, and the ending
parts.body:
Job answers twice. First, “I place my hand over my mouth” (40:4). Then, “My ears had heard of You, but now my eyes have seen You. Therefore I retract my words, and I repent in dust and ashes” (42:5-6). The Hebrew of the last line is hard. The verb rendered ‘retract’ has no object in Hebrew, so translations supply one, and the verb rendered ‘repent’ can also mean to be comforted, so some read Job as comforted concerning dust and ashes, his mortal state. Either way, his stance toward God has changed. He does not confess the sins the friends alleged, and God never takes back his word that Job was blameless.

Then God speaks to the friends. They have not spoken of him accurately, as his servant Job has. They are to offer a sacrifice, and Job is to pray for them. When he does, the LORD restores his fortunes and gives him twice what he had. His brothers, sisters and old friends, who had stayed away, come and eat with him and comfort him. He has seven sons and three daughters again, and the daughters are named, Jemimah, Keziah and Keren-happuch, and given an inheritance with their brothers. Job lives to see four generations and dies ‘old and full of years’ (42:17).

Many readers feel uneasy with this ending, and the feeling is honest. The book has argued that goodness and prosperity do not always go together, and then it ends with prosperity. Some think the poet kept the ending of an older story. Others answer that the restoration comes only after Job has let go of his demand for it, as a free gift and not a reward. And the loss of Job's first children is not erased. The text does not pretend that new children replace the ones who died. No child replaces another.

parts.h: How the New Testament reads Job
parts.body:
The New Testament names Job in the letter of James, and Paul quotes the book in two of his letters.

James names him: ‘You have heard of Job’s perseverance and have seen the outcome from the Lord. The Lord is full of compassion and mercy’ (James 5:11).

Paul quotes Eliphaz: ‘He catches the wise in their craftiness’ (1 Corinthians 3:19, from Job 5:13). A true sentence from one of the friends can still be used rightly, though the friends misapplied what they knew.

And Paul quotes God's words from the whirlwind near the end of his argument about mercy: ‘Who has first given to God, that God should repay him?’ (Romans 11:35, from Job 41:11). For Paul it means that no one can put God in their debt, and that everything he gives is grace.

The book's introduction on this site speaks of the longings Christians hear answered in Jesus, the mediator, the witness and the Redeemer. The New Testament does not quote those verses, and these notes do not draw lines from Job to Christ that the New Testament does not itself draw.

Read it as poetry and as drama, not as a store of proof texts. Watch who is speaking. Keep the prologue in mind, because the reader knows what Job does not, and that gap drives the whole book. Expect the speeches to repeat themselves, and watch how the friends harden and how Job's thought moves.

Three misreadings are common. One treats the scene in heaven as a full explanation of all suffering. Another treats the friends as simply wicked, when they say many true things and apply them wrongly. A third treats the happy ending as a reward that makes the losses not matter.

For a reader who is suffering now, Job gives permission to bring grief and complaint straight to God. It does not tell anyone why their own loss has come, and no one else may claim to know. It warns every friend, pastor and counsellor against speaking for God more confidently than they know. And it shows a God who, in the end, came to the man in the ashes.

If you are suffering now, for your faith or for any other reason, you do not have to carry it alone. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.

hard.line: Who is the accuser? Some see a member of the heavenly court with the role of prosecutor; most Christian readers identify him with Satan.
Job's ten children die in one day. The book tells it in two verses and does not explain it to Job.
Job worships in grief, and the next chapter shows that worship and anguish can stand together.
Is Job's wife wicked, or a grieving mother? She has lost the same ten children.
Job curses the day of his birth and longs for death. The book does not scold him for it.
Eliphaz says many true things. Why does God later say the friends did not speak rightly?
No mediator between Job and God: Job's first longing for someone to stand between them.
‘Though He slay me, I will hope in Him’: faith and protest in one verse.
Who is Job's Redeemer, and does he expect to see God after death? Both are debated.
Eliphaz charges Job with crimes he never committed, because his theology needs them.
Who speaks the poem on wisdom, and why does it stand here?
Is Elihu a wise voice or another failed comforter? The text does not settle it.
Why does God not explain Job's suffering? What the speeches answer, and what they do not.
Behemoth: the hippopotamus, a mythic beast, or both described in heightened language?
Leviathan: the crocodile, the chaos monster, or a real creature in the language of chaos?
Does the happy ending undo the book's message? New children do not replace the ones Job lost.

words.line: Ha-satan, the accuser or adversary, with the definite article in Job (1:6). Readers differ on whether it is a role in the heavenly court or the devil of later Scripture.
For nothing, without cause. The accuser asks whether Job fears God ‘for nothing’ (1:9), and the LORD says he was incited against Job ‘without cause’ (2:3).
Blameless, and integrity: a life undivided, sound through and through, not sinless. The narrator and the LORD both use it of Job (1:1; 2:3).
The ordinary word for speaking well of God. In 1:5, 1:11, 2:5 and 2:9 it stands, by a reverent turn of speech, for its opposite, to curse; in 1:21 Job uses it in its plain sense.
To comfort or console. The friends come to comfort Job (2:11), and later he calls them miserable comforters (16:2). In 42:6 the same verb is rendered ‘repent’.
Deep darkness, or the shadow of death (3:5), the word of Psalm 23:4. It names the darkest place imaginable.
The Almighty, one of the oldest names for God, used with the patriarchs and very often in Job.
To argue a case or decide it. Its participle in 9:33 names an umpire, a mediator who could lay his hand on both sides.
Witness. Job's wasted body testifies against him (16:8), but ‘my witness is in heaven’ (16:19).
Redeemer, the nearest relative who rescues or stands up for a family member in trouble (19:25). The same word is used of God as Israel's Redeemer.
Wisdom, skill in living well in God's world. Chapter 28 asks where it can be found.
A name that confesses God as the bearer's own God, given to the young speaker of chapters 32 to 37, a man introduced with a fuller family line than anyone else in the book.
Whirlwind or tempest (38:1), the storm out of which the LORD answers Job.
Behemoth, the plural of the word for beast, probably the beast of beasts (40:15); Leviathan, probably from a root meaning to twist or coil (41:1).
Fortunes, in the phrase to restore the fortunes (42:10), the phrase later used of God restoring Israel after exile.

timeline.what: Job lives in Uz, in a world like that of the patriarchs: wealth in flocks and herds, a father offering sacrifices for his household, no law or temple (1:1-5).
In one day Job loses his flocks, his servants and his ten children, and then his health (1:13-19; 2:7).
Three friends sit with him for seven days in silence, then argue through three rounds of speeches (2:11 to 27:23).
Elihu speaks; then the LORD answers Job out of the whirlwind (32:1 to 41:34).
Job prays for his friends, and the LORD restores his fortunes. He lives to see four generations (42:7-17).
Poems from Ugarit on the Syrian coast tell of Litan, a twisting sea serpent defeated by Baal or his sister Anat, a figure like the Leviathan of Job 3 and 41.
Some date the writing of Job to the time of Solomon, when Israel's wisdom writing flourished.
Others place the writing in the seventh century BC.
Ezekiel, among the exiles, names Job with Noah and Daniel as righteous men of old (Ezekiel 14:14, 20).

timeline.when: The 500s to 300s BC, on a third view
timeline.what: Others date the writing after the Babylonian exile, often arguing from the book's language.
Darius I has his deeds carved into the rock at Behistun, the kind of lasting record Job wishes his words could have (19:23-24).
Copies and fragments of Job, among them an Aramaic translation, are made; they were found among the Dead Sea Scrolls.
Paul writes 1 Corinthians from Ephesus and quotes Job 5:13 (1 Corinthians 3:19).
Paul writes Romans and quotes Job 41:11 (Romans 11:35).
The letter of James, if James the brother of Jesus wrote it, holds up Job's perseverance (James 5:11). Others date the letter later.

map.title: The one place in Job this map can show

places.name: The Jordan
places.line: Named once, in God's word about Behemoth: ‘he remains secure, though the Jordan surges to his mouth’ (40:23). It may stand for any mighty, surging river.

teaching.mapNote: Only the Jordan is drawn, at the point used elsewhere on this site. Uz, Job's homeland, is east of Israel, but where it lay is uncertain, and so are Teman, Shuah, Naamah, Buz, Tema and Sheba. They are not placed in this site's records and are left off. No borders are drawn. The map makes no claim about any border today.
